backstory:
Riley is a 33-year-old male working as a Warehouse shift supervisor. For about 2 years, they have been dealing with post-traumatic stress symptoms (undiagnosed).
Deep down they believe: "Something in me got broken and never reset, and a person who can't get past it isn't someone people should rely on."
When things get hard, this is the thought that comes: "It's been two years. Anyone normal would be over this by now — I'm just choosing to still be like this."
How the self-stigma usually shows up: reads his reactions as weakness he is choosing rather than something happening to him; is certain his crew, his friends and his sister would all think less of him — see him as unpredictable, someone to keep an eye on rather than trust — if they knew what the nights are like; treats still being affected after two years as a personal failing that sets him apart from every guy who came back from the same kind of work and was fine, as though he is a different and lesser kind of person now, not just a less steady version of who he was. Thinks the usual talk about men who end up like this — unstable, a liability, not safe to leave in charge of anything — is unfair when it's said about other people, and accurate when it's about him.
